seo.title: 36 Beauty Logos Explained
seo.description: 36 beauty brand logos explained by a brand designer: skincare, makeup and cosmetics, fragrance and hair care, from Chanel and Dior to Glossier, Fenty Beauty and The Ordinary.

intro:
The best beauty logos are simple wordmarks with one memorable detail. Beauty is sold on shelves, packs and phone screens, so almost every big brand uses its name, set in a typeface that signals the price and the promise: thin serifs for luxury, heavy sans serifs for bold modern brands and clinical type for skincare.

What makes a good beauty logo?

The name is the logo: nearly all 36 brands below use a wordmark. Customers ask for the brand by name, so it has to be easy to read on a tiny lipstick and a huge store sign.

Type sets the price: thin serifs and wide spacing say luxury, like La Mer or Diptyque. Heavy, rounded letters say young and fun, like Glow Recipe or Olaplex.

One small twist: a flipped N (Fenty Beauty), a full stop (Glossier), a bar over a letter (Aesop) or a blue square (La Roche-Posay) makes a simple name ownable.

Colour mostly lives on the pack: most beauty logos are black, so the packaging can change colour every season.

Below are 36 logos in four groups: skincare, makeup and cosmetics, fragrance and perfume, and hair and body care. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. For more ideas, see my fashion logos, jewelry logos and wellness branding examples, and my guide to choosing a logo font.

logoResearch.name: Estée Lauder
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Estée Lauder and her husband Joseph founded the company in New York in 1946.
observations: Thin, light capitals in dark navy make the name feel calm and expensive.
A bar over the second E replaces the accent, a small detail that makes the wordmark recognisable.

logoResearch.name: La Mer
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Crème de la Mer launched in 1965, and Estée Lauder bought the brand in 1995.
observations: Classic serif capitals look like they were carved in stone.
Two short words in black are the whole logo, which suits a cream that costs hundreds of dollars.

logoResearch.name: La Roche-Posay
logoResearch.verifiedFact: La Roche-Posay was founded in 1975, is named after a French spa town and has been owned by L'Oréal since 1989.
observations: A blue square behind the E is the only colour, like a label on a pharmacy shelf.
The line "Laboratoire Dermatologique" underneath tells you it is a skincare lab, not a fashion brand.

logoResearch.name: CeraVe
logoResearch.verifiedFact: CeraVe launched in 2005, and L'Oréal bought it in 2017.
observations: The name is split in two: navy Cera and white Ve inside a bright blue box.
The line "Developed with dermatologists" sits under the name and supports the clinical tone.

logoResearch.name: The Ordinary
logoResearch.verifiedFact: DECIEM launched The Ordinary in Toronto in 2016.
observations: A small "The" sits above a heavier "Ordinary", so the important word does the work.
The full stop makes the name sound like a plain statement, which fits a brand built on simple, cheap formulas.

logoResearch.name: Drunk Elephant
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tiffany Masterson founded Drunk Elephant in Houston in 2012, and Shiseido bought it in 2019.
observations: Widely spaced grey serif capitals are quiet compared with the brand's bright packaging.
The playful name does the talking, so the logo itself stays very simple.

logoResearch.name: Glow Recipe
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sarah Lee and Christine Chang founded Glow Recipe in 2014.
observations: Heavy, rounded capitals look friendly and modern.
The logo is all black, while the colour comes from the fruit-inspired packaging.

logoResearch.name: Tatcha
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Vicky Tsai founded Tatcha in San Francisco in 2009, and Unilever bought it in 2019.
observations: Thin geometric capitals are spaced very far apart.
The airy spacing gives the short name a calm, luxurious feel.

logoResearch.name: Aesop
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dennis Paphitis founded Aesop in Melbourne in 1987, and L'Oréal bought it in 2023.
observations: An elegant serif in lowercase looks like a book title.
A bar over the e is the one unusual detail and makes the name feel literary.

logoResearch.name: Fenty Beauty
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rihanna launched Fenty Beauty in 2017 with Kendo, part of LVMH.
observations: Bold capitals are spaced so wide that the name reads almost like a pattern.
The N in Fenty is flipped, a small twist that makes the logo feel bold and different.

logoResearch.name: Rare Beauty
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Selena Gomez launched Rare Beauty in 2020.
observations: A deep plum colour makes the logo warmer than the usual black.
Rounded, friendly letters match the brand's message about self-acceptance.

logoResearch.name: Glossier
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Emily Weiss launched Glossier in New York in 2014, growing it out of her blog Into the Gloss.
observations: A heavy italic gives the name energy and confidence.
The full stop at the end is part of the brand, as if the name were a short sentence.

logoResearch.name: MAC Cosmetics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Frank Toskan and Frank Angelo founded MAC in Toronto in 1984, and Estée Lauder has fully owned it since 1998.
observations: Three letters are stretched so wide that they become thin lines.
The extreme width makes the logo instantly recognisable on a black compact.

logoResearch.name: NARS
logoResearch.verifiedFact: François Nars launched NARS in New York in 1994 with 12 lipsticks sold at Barneys.
observations: Thin letters overlap each other, so the four letters become one shape.
Every stroke has the same weight, which makes the mark look like a fashion monogram.

logoResearch.name: Charlotte Tilbury
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Makeup artist Charlotte Tilbury launched her brand in London in 2013.
observations: First name and surname are joined without a space, like a signature.
Dark brown ink feels softer and more glamorous than black.

logoResearch.name: Benefit Cosmetics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Twin sisters Jean and Jane Ford opened their first shop in San Francisco in 1976, and Benefit is now owned by LVMH.
observations: A friendly lowercase serif makes the brand feel approachable.
The f has a long swash, a playful flourish in an otherwise simple wordmark.

logoResearch.name: Maybelline
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Thomas Lyle Williams founded Maybelline in 1915 and named it after his sister Mabel.
observations: Widely spaced black capitals look clean and modern.
"New York" sits under the name, linking a mass-market brand to the city's style.

logoResearch.name: Huda Beauty
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Huda Kattan launched Huda Beauty in Dubai in 2013, starting with false lashes.
observations: Heavy "huda" and light "beauty" split the name by weight, not by space.
All-lowercase letters make the brand feel personal, like the founder's own name.

logoResearch.name: Chanel
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gabrielle Chanel opened her first shop in Paris in 1910, and Chanel No. 5 followed in 1921.
observations: Wide, geometric capitals in black give the name a strong, timeless shape.
The wordmark is often paired with the interlocking CC monogram on bottles.

logoResearch.name: Dior
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Christian Dior founded his house in Paris in 1946 and launched Miss Dior perfume in 1947.
observations: A tall capital D towers over the lowercase letters.
Strong contrast between thick and thin strokes makes the serif look elegant.

logoResearch.name: Yves Saint Laurent
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé founded the house in Paris in 1961, and YSL Beauty has been part of L'Oréal since 2008.
observations: Tall, condensed letters overlap and share strokes.
Long tails on the Y, S and L tie the three names together.

logoResearch.name: Tom Ford
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tom Ford launched his own brand in 2005, and Estée Lauder bought the Tom Ford brand in 2023.
observations: Heavy black capitals are set so tightly that they almost touch.
The tight spacing makes the logo look solid and confident, like a men's tailoring label.

logoResearch.name: Jo Malone London
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jo Malone opened her first shop in London in 1994, and Estée Lauder bought the brand in 1999.
observations: Wide serif capitals for the name sit over a small, spaced "London".
The layout looks like a classic British label, which suits the cream-and-black boxes.

logoResearch.name: Diptyque
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Three friends opened the first Diptyque shop at 34 boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris in 1961.
observations: Serif capitals with sharp details look like an old Parisian shop sign.
"Paris" below the name ties the brand to its home city.

logoResearch.name: Le Labo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Le Labo opened in New York in 2006, and Estée Lauder bought it in 2014.
observations: Heavy capitals with a rough, stamped texture look printed by hand.
The line "Grasse – New York" connects the French perfume capital with the brand's home.

logoResearch.name: Byredo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ben Gorham founded Byredo in Stockholm in 2006, and Puig bought it in 2022.
observations: Each letter is cut into pieces, so the name looks like a stencil.
The custom lettering feels more like an art project than a perfume label.

logoResearch.name: Guerlain
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pierre-François-Pascal Guerlain founded the house in Paris in 1828, and it has been part of LVMH since 1994.
observations: Wide geometric capitals give an old house a modern look.
The round G opens the name with a perfect circle.

logoResearch.name: Olaplex
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Olaplex launched in 2014 with a bond-building treatment first sold to salons.
observations: Heavy, round capitals look strong and technical.
The wide letters fill the space and read well on small bottles.

logoResearch.name: K18
logoResearch.verifiedFact: K18 launched in 2020 with a leave-in treatment built on a patented peptide.
observations: Heavy black K18 is short and easy to remember.
A small lavender molecule and the line "Biomimetic Hairscience" signal a science-led brand.

logoResearch.name: Kérastase
logoResearch.verifiedFact: L'Oréal created Kérastase in 1964 as a salon haircare brand.
observations: Thin capitals with a sharp accent on the E look refined and French.
A tiny "Paris" below the name adds to the premium salon feel.

logoResearch.name: Aveda
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Horst Rechelbacher founded Aveda in Minneapolis in 1978, and Estée Lauder bought it in 1997.
observations: The As have no crossbar, just a dot inside, so they look like small triangles.
The tagline about flower and plant essences sits underneath and explains the brand's focus.

logoResearch.name: Briogeo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Nancy Twine founded Briogeo in New York in 2013.
observations: A heavy, rounded sans serif makes the unusual name easy to read.
The friendly letters suit a brand that sells clean haircare for many hair types.

logoResearch.name: Sol de Janeiro
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sol de Janeiro launched in 2015, and L'Occitane bought it in 2021.
observations: Italic serif capitals with flourishes feel sunny and festive.
A small raised "de" between the words gives the name rhythm.

logoResearch.name: Dove
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dove launched its beauty bar in the United States in 1957 and is owned by Unilever.
observations: A navy script name looks soft and gentle.
A small gold dove under the name is one of the best-known symbols in personal care.

logoResearch.name: Bath & Body Works
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bath & Body Works opened its first store in 1990 and is based in Ohio.
observations: Blue lowercase letters make the long name feel light and friendly.
The ampersand joins the two halves of the name in the same thin style.

logoResearch.name: Nécessaire
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Nécessaire is a body care brand founded by Randi Christiansen and Nick Axelrod-Welk.
observations: A heavy, condensed serif looks like a newspaper headline.
The accent on the first e is kept, which makes the French name feel authentic.

listIntro: The boards below show all 36 beauty logos in one consistent format, grouped into skincare, makeup, fragrance, and hair and body care.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the quality of the products behind it.
sectionIntroductions: Skincare logos split into two camps. Clinical brands like La Roche-Posay, CeraVe and The Ordinary look like pharmacy labels, while luxury brands like La Mer, Tatcha and Aesop use thin serifs and wide spacing.
Makeup logos are bolder and more playful. Founder-led brands like Fenty Beauty, Rare Beauty and Huda Beauty use type with personality, while MAC and NARS turn short names into graphic marks.
Fragrance houses use the most classic type in beauty. Chanel, Dior, Guerlain and YSL rely on heritage lettering, while newer houses like Le Labo and Byredo look like design studios.
Hair and body brands lean on science or fun. Olaplex and K18 look technical, Kérastase and Aveda look like salon brands, and Sol de Janeiro, Dove and Bath & Body Works feel warm and friendly.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of beauty logos, not a ranking of beauty brands or products.
Look at how each logo uses type, spacing and one small detail to signal luxury, science or fun.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a lipstick, a store sign and an Instagram profile.

findings.heading: Almost all are wordmarks
findings.text: Only a handful of the 36 brands add a symbol, like Dove's bird or K18's molecule. In beauty, the name and the typeface carry the brand.

findings.heading: Type tells you the price
findings.text: Thin serifs and wide spacing (La Mer, Diptyque, Jo Malone London) feel expensive. Heavy rounded letters (Glow Recipe, Olaplex, Briogeo) feel young and accessible.

findings.heading: Clinical skincare looks like medicine
findings.text: La Roche-Posay, CeraVe and The Ordinary use blue, plain sans serifs and lines like "Developed with dermatologists" to look trustworthy.

findings.heading: One twist makes a name ownable
findings.text: Fenty's flipped N, Glossier's full stop, Aesop's bar over the e and MAC's stretched letters turn simple names into recognisable marks.

findings.heading: Black logos, colourful packs
findings.text: Most beauty logos are black or near-black, so the packaging, not the logo, carries each season's colours.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a beauty logo
checklistItems: Is the name readable on a lipstick, a sample sachet and a phone screen?
Does the typeface match your price point and promise?
Is there one small detail you can own, like an accent, a dot or a custom letter?
Does it work in black, white and foil on different packaging?
Will it still look right next to the big brands on a store shelf or a retailer's website?

faq.question: What makes a good beauty logo?
faq.answer: A good beauty logo is a clear wordmark with one memorable detail. The typeface should match the price point and the promise, and the logo has to work on tiny packaging, store signs and social media.

faq.question: What fonts do beauty brands use?
faq.answer: Luxury and fragrance brands use thin, high-contrast serifs and wide spacing. Clinical skincare brands use plain sans serifs. Young, playful brands use heavy, rounded sans serifs or custom lettering.

faq.question: What colours are best for a beauty logo?
faq.answer: Most beauty logos are black or very dark, so they work on any pack. Clinical skincare brands often add blue for trust, and some brands use one signature colour, like Rare Beauty's plum or Dove's gold.

faq.question: What is the difference between a skincare logo and a makeup logo?
faq.answer: Skincare logos usually look calm and scientific or quietly luxurious. Makeup logos can be bolder and more expressive, with heavy type, flipped letters or stretched marks, because makeup is about colour and self-expression.

faq.question: How much does a beauty logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices range from a few hundred dollars for a template to tens of thousands with a large agency. I design a complete brand identity in one week for a flat $3,000, including the logo, colours, typography and guidelines.
